2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/docmost/docmost
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: docmost/docmost:0.95.0 (plus redis:8.10.0-alpine)
7	  port: 3000
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"

12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: docmost
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ CLAIM THE WORKSPACE. WHOEVER COMPLETES SETUP FIRST OWNS THIS INSTANCE, PERMANENTLY. POST /api/auth/setup carries no authentication guard and is protected only by SetupGuard, which lets the request through while the workspace count is 0 and throws 403 'Workspace setup already completed.' from then on (apps/server/src/core/auth/guards/setup.guard.ts). It is anonymous-reachable and ONE-SHOT: the first person to complete it becomes the workspace owner and there is no second chance and no recovery path. The window opens the moment redu's hostname stops answering 502, so a deploy that stops at 'the URL works' has handed a stranger a wiki on hardware you pay for. Create the owner account as part of the deploy, before you hand the URL over, and CONFIRM THE EMAIL ADDRESS WITH THE USER FIRST because it is the owner identity. The script in the body of this file proves the window is shut."
18	  - "AFTER SETUP, THERE IS NO OPEN REGISTRATION, WHICH IS THE GOOD NEWS. The auth controller's complete route list is login, setup, change-password, forgot-password, password-reset, verify-token, collab-token and logout. There is no self-serve signup endpoint in the self-hosted build at all: further users arrive only through a workspace invite, and creating an invite requires a JWT (POST /api/workspace/invites/create). So there is no registration setting to turn off afterwards. The ENTIRE exposure is the one-shot setup window above, which is exactly why it deserves the loudest quirk in this file."
19	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, BY DESIGN: the single-page app and its static assets, GET /api/health (which reports whether Postgres and Redis are up, and nothing else), POST /api/workspace/public, POST /api/workspace/check-hostname, the two invite endpoints that require a token in the body, robots.txt, and /share/<shareId>/p/<pageSlug> for pages a signed-in user has deliberately shared. Shared pages are genuinely world-readable by URL once shared, which is the feature working, and it is per-share rather than a global default. Nothing else answers without a session cookie."
20	  - "⛔⛔ THE MIGRATIONS CREATE POSTGRES EXTENSIONS, SO PASS db_superuser true. This is the quirk most likely to kill the deploy outright. The migration named add-unaccent-pg_trm-update-tsvector runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent and CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm unconditionally, and migrations run automatically at every boot in production (database.module.ts onApplicationBootstrap; the image's start script sets NODE_ENV=production). migration.service.ts calls process.exit(1) when a migration errors, so a refused CREATE EXTENSION means a crash-looping container and a hostname that answers 502 forever, with the real reason visible only in the container log. Both extensions have been TRUSTED since PostgreSQL 13, so a database owner may be able to create them without superuser, but that is UNVERIFIED against redu's managed role: pass db_superuser true and the doubt goes away. Measured across all 48 migration files at v0.95.0: exactly those two CREATE EXTENSION statements, ZERO CREATE DATABASE and ZERO CREATE SCHEMA, with 40 createTable calls as the control proving the grep worked. So Docmost never hits redu's one-database-per-managed-Postgres limit."
21	  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET, AND THEN NEVER CHANGE IT. It must be at least 32 characters and must not be the placeholder string upstream ships; environment.validation.ts enforces both with @MinLength(32) and @IsNotIn, prints the failed constraints and calls process.exit(1). So unlike most apps in this library, a MISSING secret fails loudly and you cannot deploy without noticing. What is silent is CHANGING it: it signs the auth cookie, so a redeploy with a fresh value logs every user out with no error anywhere. Generate one long random value (their .env.example suggests openssl rand -hex 32), record it with the user, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy."
22	  - "⛔ DATABASE_URL AND REDIS_URL ARE BOTH MANDATORY, AND THERE IS NO SQLITE FALLBACK TO WORRY ABOUT. Both are @IsNotEmpty and protocol-validated in environment.validation.ts, so a missing or malformed value exits 1 at boot rather than quietly using a local file. redu injects a variable called literally DATABASE_URL in the postgresql:// form Docmost wants, so there is no name mapping to get wrong; just remember deploy_compose only APPENDS to the project .env and never edits your compose, so the compose must interpolate ${DATABASE_URL} itself. PROVE IT AFTER BOOT WITH A POSITIVE CHECK, not an absence: GET /api/health pings BOTH datastores (integrations/health/health.controller.ts) and returns a database entry and a redis entry, so one 200 proves the whole wiring. Then, if you want the second half, run sudo docker exec <container> printenv DATABASE_URL and confirm it names the private database VM. The VM runs docker, not podman."
23	  - "SSL ON THE DATABASE, AND ONE HELPER THAT SILENTLY REWRITES YOUR URL. Docmost passes DATABASE_URL through normalizePostgresUrl (common/helpers/utils.ts:122-134), which drops the schema parameter (their own .env.example includes one) and DROPS sslmode=no-verify entirely. So no-verify is not a way to skip certificate checks here; it just disappears. redu's injected URL carries no query string at all. Over redu's private network that is survivable, and appending ?sslmode=require is the deliberate choice. Say which you picked in the handover."
24	  - "⛔ DELETE THE db SERVICE FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE, KEEP THE redis ONE. Their docker-compose.yml ships a postgres:18 with a placeholder password, and running it alongside a redu managed Postgres means paying for two databases while the app talks to one. Remove the service and its depends_on entry. Redis is different and STAYS: Docmost genuinely requires it (the websocket adapter connects to it during bootstrap and the health endpoint pings it), but it holds queues, cache and live-collaboration state rather than a system of record, so losing it on a redeploy costs a queue drain and no documents. Keeping it in the compose also avoids a second managed datastore on the bill. Keep upstream's --maxmemory-policy noeviction: it is deliberate, because evicting queue keys under memory pressure loses jobs silently."
25	  - "⛔ MOUNT A NAMED VOLUME ON /app/data/storage, AND MAKE IT NAMED RATHER THAN A BIND MOUNT. STORAGE_DRIVER defaults to local (environment.service.ts:83), so every uploaded file, image and attachment lives on the app VM's filesystem while Postgres holds only the pages that reference them. The Dockerfile declares VOLUME [\"/app/data/storage\"], which means a compose that mounts nothing there gets an ANONYMOUS volume and loses every attachment on the next redeploy while the pages survive and render broken. Use a named volume specifically, because the image runs as USER node: a bind mount created by root on the host gives permission errors on upload, while a named volume inherits the image's ownership of that directory."
26	  - "SET APP_URL TO THE REAL PUBLIC URL BEFORE FIRST BOOT. It defaults to http://localhost:<port> (environment.service.ts:19-20) and it is what invite links, share links and every e-mail are built from, so leaving it wrong produces links that work for nobody and it is not obvious until someone clicks one. Generate the dname yourself in the full docmost-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form so the value is known at deploy time; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match."
27	  - "PORT 3000, PUBLISHED AS 3000. The Dockerfile exposes 3000 and PORT defaults to 3000. Pass 3000 to deploy_compose. There is nothing else to publish: the client, the API and the websocket all ride the same port. COLLAB_URL exists for running the collaboration server as a SEPARATE process at scale and is not needed here; one container is the supported single-VM shape and is what upstream's own compose does."
28	  - "⛔ PIN THE IMAGE, AND KNOW THAT THE NEWEST TAGS ARE BETAS. The newest STABLE image is docmost/docmost:0.95.0 (published 2026-07-04), and latest and 0.95 resolve to the same digest today. The registry also carries 0.96.0-beta-1, 0.96.0-beta-2, 0.96.0-cf.beta.1, 0.95.0-cf.beta.3 and 0.95.1-beta.2, every one of them NEWER by date and HIGHER by version number than the stable, so any tooling that sorts the tag list and takes the top one installs a beta of a wiki. Pin docmost/docmost:0.95.0 explicitly. Pin the cache too: redis:8.10.0-alpine, because upstream's compose says redis:8, which is a rolling tag that will move under you."
29	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED, AND THE FIRST BOOT IS THE SLOW ONE. The container runs its own kysely migrations at startup in production and logs each one by name. On a fresh managed Postgres that is 48 migrations plus two extension creations before the app serves anything, so give the health check room; an impatient probe reports a failed deploy on a stack that is starting normally."
30	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. Checked the README, .env.example, the compose and the Dockerfile: there is no memory figure anywhere. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is reasoning from 'one Node 26 server with a large production dependency tree serving a prebuilt client, plus a small Redis on the same VM', not a measurement. It is exactly AT the no-card trial ceiling, so a trial user can deploy this, with the one allowed managed database at m1.small. DATABASE_MAX_POOL defaults to 10 (environment.service.ts:52), which is sane against an m1.small database; leave it alone unless you measure a reason. Measure the memory on your run and write the real figure back."
31	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> generate the dname yourself and set APP_URL to https://<that>.redu.cloud -> generate APP_SECRET -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2', db_superuser:true, port 3000, compose_engine docker. Pass db_flavor_id explicitly: omitting it defaults the database VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill. plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large, which is the right default for things that BUILD from source and wrong here, since both images are pulled; passing flavor_id '3' holds m1.medium."
32	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, and the repo is a large pnpm monorepo you have no reason to clone. Write the trimmed two-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo."
33	  - "LICENCE: AGPL-3.0 FOR THE APP, PLUS A SEPARATE ENTERPRISE LICENCE OVER THE ee DIRECTORIES, AND BOTH MATTER. The repository LICENSE is the canonical GNU AGPL-3.0. Alongside it, packages/ee/LICENSE and apps/client/src/ee/LICENSE are the Docmost Enterprise License, which permits use in production only with a valid paid subscription; license-check.service.ts gates those features on a workspace licence key and returns false when there is none, so an unlicensed instance simply runs the community feature set. Two practical statements for the user. One: running the community edition unmodified, for yourself and the people you invite, is fine and is what this recipe does. Two: AGPL section 13 is a NETWORK clause, so if you MODIFY Docmost and let other people use it over a network, you owe those users your modified source. Pulling the official image unchanged triggers nothing extra. Do not switch on enterprise features without a subscription."
34	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres so the pages survive, and that database keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. ⚠️ The /app/data/storage VOLUME goes with the app VM, so every uploaded file and image is destroyed while the pages referencing them survive and render broken. Redis goes with it too, which costs nothing. Say all of that plainly before deleting, and use delete_database when the user really means all of it."

repo: https://github.com/docmost/docmost
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: docmost/docmost:0.95.0 (plus redis:8.10.0-alpine)

  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2") with db_superuser true
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: docmost
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ CLAIM THE WORKSPACE. WHOEVER COMPLETES SETUP FIRST OWNS THIS INSTANCE, PERMANENTLY. POST /api/auth/setup carries no authentication guard and is protected only by SetupGuard, which lets the request through while the workspace count is 0 and throws 403 'Workspace setup already completed.' from then on (apps/server/src/core/auth/guards/setup.guard.ts). It is anonymous-reachable and ONE-SHOT: the first person to complete it becomes the workspace owner and there is no second chance and no recovery path. The window opens the moment redu's hostname stops answering 502, so a deploy that stops at 'the URL works' has handed a stranger a wiki on hardware you pay for. Create the owner account as part of the deploy, before you hand the URL over, and CONFIRM THE EMAIL ADDRESS WITH THE USER FIRST because it is the owner identity. The script in the body of this file proves the window is shut."
  - "AFTER SETUP, THERE IS NO OPEN REGISTRATION, WHICH IS THE GOOD NEWS. The auth controller's complete route list is login, setup, change-password, forgot-password, password-reset, verify-token, collab-token and logout. There is no self-serve signup endpoint in the self-hosted build at all: further users arrive only through a workspace invite, and creating an invite requires a JWT (POST /api/workspace/invites/create). So there is no registration setting to turn off afterwards. The ENTIRE exposure is the one-shot setup window above, which is exactly why it deserves the loudest quirk in this file."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH, BY DESIGN: the single-page app and its static assets, GET /api/health (which reports whether Postgres and Redis are up, and nothing else), POST /api/workspace/public, POST /api/workspace/check-hostname, the two invite endpoints that require a token in the body, robots.txt, and /share/<shareId>/p/<pageSlug> for pages a signed-in user has deliberately shared. Shared pages are genuinely world-readable by URL once shared, which is the feature working, and it is per-share rather than a global default. Nothing else answers without a session cookie."
  - "⛔⛔ THE MIGRATIONS CREATE POSTGRES EXTENSIONS, SO PASS db_superuser true. This is the quirk most likely to kill the deploy outright. The migration named add-unaccent-pg_trm-update-tsvector runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent and CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm unconditionally, and migrations run automatically at every boot in production (database.module.ts onApplicationBootstrap; the image's start script sets NODE_ENV=production). migration.service.ts calls process.exit(1) when a migration errors, so a refused CREATE EXTENSION means a crash-looping container and a hostname that answers 502 forever, with the real reason visible only in the container log. Both extensions have been TRUSTED since PostgreSQL 13, so a database owner may be able to create them without superuser, but that is UNVERIFIED against redu's managed role: pass db_superuser true and the doubt goes away. Measured across all 48 migration files at v0.95.0: exactly those two CREATE EXTENSION statements, ZERO CREATE DATABASE and ZERO CREATE SCHEMA, with 40 createTable calls as the control proving the grep worked. So Docmost never hits redu's one-database-per-managed-Postgres limit."
  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET, AND THEN NEVER CHANGE IT. It must be at least 32 characters and must not be the placeholder string upstream ships; environment.validation.ts enforces both with @MinLength(32) and @IsNotIn, prints the failed constraints and calls process.exit(1). So unlike most apps in this library, a MISSING secret fails loudly and you cannot deploy without noticing. What is silent is CHANGING it: it signs the auth cookie, so a redeploy with a fresh value logs every user out with no error anywhere. Generate one long random value (their .env.example suggests openssl rand -hex 32), record it with the user, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy."
  - "⛔ DATABASE_URL AND REDIS_URL ARE BOTH MANDATORY, AND THERE IS NO SQLITE FALLBACK TO WORRY ABOUT. Both are @IsNotEmpty and protocol-validated in environment.validation.ts, so a missing or malformed value exits 1 at boot rather than quietly using a local file. redu injects a variable called literally DATABASE_URL in the postgresql:// form Docmost wants, so there is no name mapping to get wrong; just remember deploy_compose only APPENDS to the project .env and never edits your compose, so the compose must interpolate ${DATABASE_URL} itself. PROVE IT AFTER BOOT WITH A POSITIVE CHECK, not an absence: GET /api/health pings BOTH datastores (integrations/health/health.controller.ts) and returns a database entry and a redis entry, so one 200 proves the whole wiring. Then, if you want the second half, run sudo docker exec <container> printenv DATABASE_URL and confirm it names the private database VM. The VM runs docker, not podman."
  - "SSL ON THE DATABASE, AND ONE HELPER THAT SILENTLY REWRITES YOUR URL. Docmost passes DATABASE_URL through normalizePostgresUrl (common/helpers/utils.ts:122-134), which drops the schema parameter (their own .env.example includes one) and DROPS sslmode=no-verify entirely. So no-verify is not a way to skip certificate checks here; it just disappears. redu's injected URL carries no query string at all. Over redu's private network that is survivable, and appending ?sslmode=require is the deliberate choice. Say which you picked in the handover."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE db SERVICE FROM UPSTREAM'S COMPOSE, KEEP THE redis ONE. Their docker-compose.yml ships a postgres:18 with a placeholder password, and running it alongside a redu managed Postgres means paying for two databases while the app talks to one. Remove the service and its depends_on entry. Redis is different and STAYS: Docmost genuinely requires it (the websocket adapter connects to it during bootstrap and the health endpoint pings it), but it holds queues, cache and live-collaboration state rather than a system of record, so losing it on a redeploy costs a queue drain and no documents. Keeping it in the compose also avoids a second managed datastore on the bill. Keep upstream's --maxmemory-policy noeviction: it is deliberate, because evicting queue keys under memory pressure loses jobs silently."

The Dockerfile declares VOLUME [\"/app/data/storage\"], which means a compose that mounts nothing there gets an ANONYMOUS volume and loses every attachment on the next redeploy while the pages survive and render broken. # Self-host Docmost on redu

A collaborative wiki and documentation space, on infrastructure you own: real-time editing,
permissions, page history and public share links, with your documents in a managed Postgres in the
EU rather than someone else's tenant.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## What this deploys

- **Docmost** from the official image, pinned to a stable release, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so every page, comment and permission survives a
  redeploy.
- **Redis** alongside the app, for queues, caching and live collaboration. It holds no documents.
- A volume on `/app/data/storage`, which holds every uploaded file and image.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Docmost on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's file ships its own Postgres with a placeholder password and an `APP_SECRET` set to the
literal string the app refuses to start on. This is that file with the database removed and the
managed one wired in:

```yaml
services:
  docmost:
    image: docmost/docmost:0.95.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      - redis
    environment:
      APP_URL: "${DOCMOST_APP_URL}"
      APP_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password]"
      STORAGE_DRIVER: "local"
    volumes:
      - docmost-storage:/app/data/storage
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
  redis:
    image: redis:8.10.0-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--maxmemory-policy", "noeviction"]
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
volumes:
  docmost-storage:
  redis-data:
```

`DOCMOST_APP_URL` is `https://` plus a dname you generate before deploying. `DATABASE_URL` is
injected by redu. `APP_SECRET` is yours to generate, at least 32 characters.

## The three that actually break it

**The setup window.** `POST /api/auth/setup` has no authentication and is one-shot: the first
person to complete it owns the workspace forever. It opens the moment the hostname answers. Claim
it during the deploy, not afterwards.

**The extensions.** Docmost's migrations run `CREATE EXTENSION` for `unaccent` and `pg_trgm`
at every boot, and a migration failure exits the process. If the database role cannot create them,
the container crash-loops and the URL answers 502 forever with the real reason only in the log.
Deploy with `db_superuser: true`.

**The storage volume.** Uploaded files live on disk, not in Postgres. The image declares the
directory as a volume, so a compose that mounts nothing there gets an anonymous one and loses every
attachment on the next redeploy while the pages still reference them.

## Proving the workspace has an owner

Run this once the deploy reports ready, and run it **before** you hand anyone the URL.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Docmost has an owner and its one-shot setup window is shut.
#   ./verify-owner.sh docmost-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and closed, 1 = UNCLAIMED (claim it right now), 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-owner.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE AND POSITIVE CONTROL IN ONE. /api/health pings BOTH Postgres and Redis, so a 200 whose
#    body names them proves Docmost is what is answering AND that its datastores are wired. Without
#    this gate, redu's 502-while-starting error page sails through the assertion below.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/health")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered HTTP $code. A crash-looping container answers this way, and the
  usual cause is the CREATE EXTENSION migration being refused. Read the container log before anything else."
fi
grep -q '"database"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no database entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
grep -q '"redis"' "$TMP/health"    || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no redis entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
echo "OK: Docmost is serving and both Postgres and Redis answered."

# 2. THE ASSERTION, on behaviour rather than on a flag.
#    SetupGuard runs BEFORE body validation: it throws 403 once any workspace exists, and otherwise
#    lets the request reach the global ValidationPipe. The body below is an EMPTY object, so it can
#    never create an account either way. That is what makes 403 the safe answer and 400 the alarm.
printf '{}' > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/setup")

case "$code" in
  403)
    echo "OK: setup is closed, so a workspace and an owner already exist."
    exit 0
    ;;
  400)
    echo "FAIL: THIS INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED. The setup guard let an anonymous request through, which" >&2
    echo "means no workspace exists yet and the next person to load this URL becomes its owner," >&2
    echo "permanently. Complete setup NOW, then re-run this script." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  429)
    inconclusive "the auth throttler returned 429. Wait a minute and re-run; this proved nothing."
    ;;
  404)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404. Find the live route first: a route that
  exists but rejects the method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac
```

The app is **AGPL-3.0**. Separately, the `ee` directories in the repo are under the Docmost
Enterprise License and need a paid subscription to use in production; without a licence key the
instance simply runs the community feature set. Running the community edition unmodified, for
yourself and the people you invite, is fine. AGPL section 13 is a network clause: modify Docmost
and serve those modifications to others and you owe those users your source. Pulling the official
image unchanged does not trigger it.

| | |
|---|---|
| App VM | **m1.medium** (2 vCPU / 4 GB) — Docmost + Redis via docker compose, port 3000 |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Docmost has an owner and its one-shot setup window is shut.
#   ./verify-owner.sh docmost-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and closed, 1 = UNCLAIMED (claim it right now), 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-owner.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/health")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered HTTP $code. A crash-looping container answers this way, and the
  usual cause is the CREATE EXTENSION migration being refused. Read the container log before anything else."
fi
grep -q '"database"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no database entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
grep -q '"redis"' "$TMP/health"    || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no redis entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
echo "OK: Docmost is serving and both Postgres and Redis answered."

printf '{}' > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/setup")

case "$code" in
  403)
    echo "OK: setup is closed, so a workspace and an owner already exist."
    exit 0
    ;;
  400)
    echo "FAIL: THIS INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED. The setup guard let an anonymous request through, which" >&2
    echo "means no workspace exists yet and the next person to load this URL becomes its owner," >&2
    echo "permanently. Complete setup NOW, then re-run this script." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  429)
    inconclusive "the auth throttler returned 429. Wait a minute and re-run; this proved nothing."
    ;;
  404)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404. Find the live route first: a route that
  exists but rejects the method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac
EOF

# Self-host Docmost on redu

A collaborative wiki and documentation space, on infrastructure you own: real-time editing,
permissions, page history and public share links, with your documents in a managed Postgres in the
EU rather than someone else's tenant.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## What this deploys

- **Docmost** from the official image, pinned to a stable release, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so every page, comment and permission survives a
  redeploy.
- **Redis** alongside the app, for queues, caching and live collaboration. It holds no documents.
- A volume on `/app/data/storage`, which holds every uploaded file and image.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Docmost on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's file ships its own Postgres with a placeholder password and an `APP_SECRET` set to the
literal string the app refuses to start on. This is that file with the database removed and the
managed one wired in:

```yaml
services:
  docmost:
    image: docmost/docmost:0.95.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      - redis
    environment:
      APP_URL: "${DOCMOST_APP_URL}"
      APP_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://redis:[REDACTED:conn-password]"
      STORAGE_DRIVER: "local"
    volumes:
      - docmost-storage:/app/data/storage
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
  redis:
    image: redis:8.10.0-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--maxmemory-policy", "noeviction"]
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
volumes:
  docmost-storage:
  redis-data:
```

`DOCMOST_APP_URL` is `https://` plus a dname you generate before deploying. `DATABASE_URL` is
injected by redu. `APP_SECRET` is yours to generate, at least 32 characters.

## The three that actually break it

**The setup window.** `POST /api/auth/setup` has no authentication and is one-shot: the first
person to complete it owns the workspace forever. It opens the moment the hostname answers. Claim
it during the deploy, not afterwards.

**The extensions.** Docmost's migrations run `CREATE EXTENSION` for `unaccent` and `pg_trgm`
at every boot, and a migration failure exits the process. If the database role cannot create them,
the container crash-loops and the URL answers 502 forever with the real reason only in the log.
Deploy with `db_superuser: true`.

**The storage volume.** Uploaded files live on disk, not in Postgres. The image declares the
directory as a volume, so a compose that mounts nothing there gets an anonymous one and loses every
attachment on the next redeploy while the pages still reference them.

## Proving the workspace has an owner

Run this once the deploy reports ready, and run it **before** you hand anyone the URL.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Docmost has an owner and its one-shot setup window is shut.
#   ./verify-owner.sh docmost-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = claimed and closed, 1 = UNCLAIMED (claim it right now), 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-owner.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE AND POSITIVE CONTROL IN ONE. /api/health pings BOTH Postgres and Redis, so a 200 whose
#    body names them proves Docmost is what is answering AND that its datastores are wired. Without
#    this gate, redu's 502-while-starting error page sails through the assertion below.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/health")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/api/health answered HTTP $code. A crash-looping container answers this way, and the
  usual cause is the CREATE EXTENSION migration being refused. Read the container log before anything else."
fi
grep -q '"database"' "$TMP/health" || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no database entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
grep -q '"redis"' "$TMP/health"    || inconclusive "/api/health returned 200 with no redis entry, so this is not Docmost's health endpoint."
echo "OK: Docmost is serving and both Postgres and Redis answered."

# 2. THE ASSERTION, on behaviour rather than on a flag.
#    SetupGuard runs BEFORE body validation: it throws 403 once any workspace exists, and otherwise
#    lets the request reach the global ValidationPipe. The body below is an EMPTY object, so it can
#    never create an account either way. That is what makes 403 the safe answer and 400 the alarm.
printf '{}' > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' \
  -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/api/auth/setup")

case "$code" in
  403)
    echo "OK: setup is closed, so a workspace and an owner already exist."
    exit 0
    ;;
  400)
    echo "FAIL: THIS INSTANCE IS UNCLAIMED. The setup guard let an anonymous request through, which" >&2
    echo "means no workspace exists yet and the next person to load this URL becomes its owner," >&2
    echo "permanently. Complete setup NOW, then re-run this script." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  429)
    inconclusive "the auth throttler returned 429. Wait a minute and re-run; this proved nothing."
    ;;
  404)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered 404, so the route moved and this probe proved nothing.
  Do not leave the instance up on the strength of a 404. Find the live route first: a route that
  exists but rejects the method answers 405, one that does not exist answers 404."
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "/api/auth/setup answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac
```

Docmost is live at **https://docmost-actvwmjn.redu.cloud** and the workspace is claimed.

**Your credentials** — record these now, they're not written to any file:

| | |
|---|---|
| Owner email | `«REDACTED:env:013044ef»` |
| Password | `«REDACTED:entropy:037158a6»` |
| `APP_SECRET` | `«REDACTED:longhex:ba82c125»` |

Change the password in the UI when you log in. **Keep the `APP_SECRET`** — it signs the auth cookie, so passing a different one on a redeploy logs everyone out silently, with no error anywhere.

**Verified, not assumed:**
- `/api/health` → 200 with `database: up` and `redis: up` — that single response proves both datastores are wired.
- `verify-owner.sh` exits 0: setup now returns **403**, so the one-shot window is shut. I claimed it 5 minutes after the container started answering, before handing you the URL.
- Owner login returns 200.
- `restarts=0`, and `add-unaccent-pg_trm-update-tsvector` logged `executed successfully` — **`db_superuser: true` is confirmed sufficient against redu's managed Postgres**, which was the open question in `redu.md`.
- Named volumes `app-src_docmost-storage` and `app-src_redis-data` exist, so attachments survive a redeploy.

**Cost: £0.0452/hr, ~£33/month** — m1.medium app VM (£0.0278) + m1.small managed Postgres (£0.0174). `plan_deploy` wanted m1.large at £48.18/mo; `flavor_id: "3"` held m1.medium as the recipe says.

Two things worth knowing:

- **Database SSL:** I took redu's injected `DATABASE_URL` as-is, with no `sslmode` — plaintext over the private network. That was the recipe's survivable option. To require TLS instead you'd have to pass your own `DATABASE_URL` in `env`, since redu appends its value to `.env` and the later duplicate wins.
- **Memory, measured for the first time:** app container 356 MiB idle, Redis 6.5 MiB, 1245 MB of 3915 MB used VM-wide. m1.medium is comfortable, not tight.

Mid-deploy the redu **control API** returned openresty 502s for a couple of minutes while the app itself kept answering 200 on its own hostname. Nothing was wrong; I've added it as a quirk so the next run doesn't mistake it for a failed deploy.

Files written: `redu.md` (last_deploy block, a full deploy-log entry, and 13 quirk edits carrying this run's measurements — the merge tool withheld its version as over-budget, so I applied them by hand and validated the YAML), `redu-deploy-plan.md` (real provisioned values, replacing the estimate), `docker-compose.yml`, and `verify-owner.sh`.

One caveat on `delete_deployment` when you're done: it removes the app VM but **deliberately leaves the managed Postgres billing at £0.0174/hr**, and the storage volume dies with the VM — so uploaded files are destroyed while the pages referencing them survive and render broken. Use `delete_database` too if you mean all of it.
